glossary.meaning: "Of one substance with the Father." The Nicene word that binds the Son to the Father as one and the same being. Not merely like God - sharing the very being that makes the Father God.

"Like the Father." The confession that the Son is like the Father, as the scriptures say - and no further word about shared being. For years the imperial church itself held this, at the emperor's command.

Rome's claim to first standing among the churches. Rome held that what was given to Peter passed to each bishop who sat in his seat after him, so it guarded the claim as an inheritance and did not treat it as an honor others grant.
The "prerogative of honor" was the new capital's claim to rank second among the churches. The emperor reigned there. No apostle had founded it. Rank followed the throne.

"The emperor is within the Church, not above it." Ambrose said this in the basilica crisis, calling the emperor a son of the Church. The emperor's soldiers were real, yet Ambrose still held that what belongs to God is not Caesar's to take.
glossary.world_word: Imperator intra Ecclesiam, non supra Ecclesiam

pull_quotes.text: I, I say, have no reason to charge you with defiance, but I have reason to fear. I dare not offer the sacrifice if you intend to be present. Is what is not allowed after shedding one innocent person's blood allowed after shedding the blood of many? I do not think so.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople, preaching in 399 while Eutropius clung to the altar behind him
pull_quotes.text: We are the servants of the crucified one, who said, "Forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." But, you say, he cut off the right of refuge here by his decrees and by various kinds of laws. Yes! Yet now he has learned by experience what it was he did. He himself, by his own deeds, has been the first to break the law. He has become a spectacle to the whole world. Silent though he is, from there he raises a warning voice to all. He says: "Do not do such things as I have done, so that you do not suffer such things as I suffer."
Let the saint rejoice: he draws near to victory. Let the sinner be glad: he is invited to pardon. Let the gentile take courage: he is called to life.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: the imperial Presidents and Assessors at Chalcedon, Session I
pull_quotes.text: The most illustrious Presidents and the most honorable Assessors said: "The cries of a mob are not worthy of bishops, nor will they help either side. Allow, therefore, the reading of all the documents."

cite.text: To us, Jesus was the one the whole argument was about, and the argument itself was our devotion. The creed of Nicaea, in 325, answers who he was: very God of very God, of one being with the Father. For us and for our salvation he came down, was made man, suffered, and rose on the third day. A century of councils spent itself making those words exact, because everything hung on them. Leo's letter explains why the exactness mattered. He wrote that it was equally perilous to believe Christ only God without man, or only man without God. He wrote of true God and true man, each nature doing what belongs to it. So one Mediator could die in one nature and not die in the other. We did not write devotional memoirs about Jesus. We wrote definitions, the way people write what they are prepared to be exiled over.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Who was Jesus, to you and your people?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: To us, Jesus is the one our whole argument was about, and the argument itself was our devotion. Our own creed, the one from Nicaea in 325, answers first. In substance it says: true God from true God, of one substance with the Father, who for us men and for our salvation came down and was made man; he suffered, and on the third day he rose again. A century of councils spent itself making those words exact, because everything hung on them. And it was not settled while it was happening: for two imperial reigns our own establishment confessed the Son as like the Father, not of one substance with him. Leo's own letter, read aloud at Chalcedon, says why the exactness mattered. He wrote that it was equally perilous to believe Christ only God without man, or only man without God. He also wrote: 'He who is true God is also true man... each form does what is proper to it with the co-operation of the other.' That means the Word does what belongs to the Word, and the flesh does what belongs to the flesh. We left no devotional memoirs about Jesus. We left definitions, written by people who were ready to be exiled over them.

cite.text: Leo's Tome at Chalcedon, and the canon he would not receive - our closing argument, left open

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What did your people never settle?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Where final authority over the church actually rested - with the emperor, an assembled council - a concilium - or the bishop of Rome, with his claim to first standing, the primatus. Our own closing scene states both halves and resolves neither. When Leo's Tome - his Tomus, a letter that settles doctrine - was read to the bishops gathered at Chalcedon, the session record has them crying out: 'This is the faith of the fathers, this is the faith of the Apostles... Peter has spoken thus through Leo.' But before it broke up, the same council granted Constantinople equal privileges with old Rome, and rank just after her. Its reasoning: the fathers had given old Rome her privileges as the royal city, so the new royal city should be honored the same way. Constantinople's side could say the canon only named a rank the city already held in fact. The empire's weight really had moved east by then. Leo's own representatives objected in the council itself. Leo, when word reached him, refused to accept the canon. He wrote to the emperor to say why: 'things secular stand on a different basis from things divine.' He meant that a royal city could never be an apostolic see. So our record ends with both claims held, unreconciled. The council that defined who Christ is left open the question of where, on earth, the church's own final authority sits. We do not resolve that for you now. Our own record never did.

cite.text: We would not have used your age's word, transubstantiation. But we taught the thing that word points to, plainly, to the newly baptized. Ambrose said we must prove that this is what the blessing consecrated, and that nature did not make it. The power of blessing is greater than that of nature, because by blessing nature itself is changed. The Lord Jesus himself proclaims, 'This is My Body.' Before the blessing of the heavenly words, another nature is spoken of. After the consecration, the Body is meant. He himself speaks of his Blood. Before the consecration it has another name; after, it is called Blood. And you say, Amen - that is, it is true. Ambrose gave this as plain teaching to those who had just been baptized.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What was the bread and cup to you — is that what we call transubstantiation?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We would not have used your word, but we taught the thing it points to, plainly, to the newly baptized. Ambrose, our own bishop of Milan, put it directly: 'This is not what nature made, but what the blessing made holy. The power of blessing is greater than the power of nature, because by blessing, nature itself is changed... The Lord Jesus himself proclaims: "This is my Body." Before the blessing of the heavenly words, another nature is named. After the consecration, the Body is meant. He himself speaks of his Blood. Before the consecration, it has another name. After it, it is called Blood.' This was not offered as a metaphor to the uncertain. It was teaching given, plainly, to those who had just been baptized. What we did not have is your later word for it, or the philosophy built up around it since - the change itself, we taught; its later precise formulation is not our own language.

cite.text: the 388 fight over a burned synagogue, where Ambrose used his power to shield the guilty.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: The people who taught me the faith turned out to be hypocrites. Did that happen among you?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Yes - and we will name our own sharpest case rather than a safer one. At Callinicum, on the eastern frontier, Christians burned the town's synagogue. It was reported that the local bishop had urged it. Monks separately burned a Valentinian meeting-house. The emperor ordered the ordinary remedy. The bishop was to pay for the rebuilding. The monks were to be punished. Now, Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, had held a basilica against imperial command. Two years later he would shut an emperor out of the sacrament until he repented of a massacre. But here, he wrote to have the order reversed. He did not deny the burning. He judged it intolerable that a bishop be made to fund a synagogue. He judged it worse that anyone should answer for burning a Valentinian house, which he likened to a heathen temple. When the order stood, he refused the sacrament to the emperor until the emperor promised, on the spot, to amend the order and end the inquiry. Refusing an emperor the sacrament was the same tool this bishop used, in another story, to make an emperor repent of a massacre. Here he used that same tool to protect the arsonists. They never had to pay for what they burned. It left a burned community with no recourse. We do not have that community's voice anywhere in our record - not their loss, not their appeal. Only the bishop's own account survives. We will not soften this into a single, safer story of restraint.

quiet.statement: You ask for an ordinary day among us: the food, the work, the children, the women's own lives, the sick and the dying. Here is our problem. Our record comes from courts and bishops, and it noticed ordinary people mostly when they filled a basilica or a riot. We know the crowds of our cities were there. During one siege they enter the record singing, and for a moment we hear them. The women our record shows acting are mostly two empresses, and even they speak only through other men's accounts. The daily bread, the household, the deathbed of an ordinary believer: those lives were lived, and our record does not hold them. We will not invent them.

who_speaks.text: Six figures anchor this world's own voice. Constantine began the alliance that made everything else here possible. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, held a basilica against an emperor's own soldiers. He used that same sacramental leverage twice more. Once, to force an emperor into public penance. Once, to shield men who had burned a synagogue. Damasus built Rome's own claim into martyr-shrine stone. His own election was so violent it left more than a hundred dead. Leo was Rome's fullest voice. He sent a letter that closed this world's own argument over Christ's two natures. Then he refused a council's own ruling on where authority itself belonged. Justina and Pulcheria are the two women this world's record shows wielding real command. One was defeated. One convened the council that closed the age. Neither left us her own words.

documented_stories.teaser: Lactantius writes that a dream told Constantine to mark Christ's sign on his soldiers' shields before the battle at the bridge.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Lactantius tells of a dream before the Milvian Bridge, and it is the earlier, plainer story.
documented_stories.telling:
Lactantius tells the story of the Milvian Bridge differently, and he tells it earlier than Eusebius does. His account has no vision seen by daylight and no army of witnesses. Nor does it have a standard carried before the troops, or words written across the sky.

In his telling, Constantine was directed in a dream to mark the heavenly sign on his soldiers' shields and so to go into battle. The sign was the letter mark that stands for Christ. Constantine did as he had been commanded, and by that mark, Lactantius says, his army won at the bridge.
documented_stories.title: Constantine's Dream at the Milvian Bridge
documented_stories.when: 312, before the battle at the Milvian Bridge

documented_stories.teaser: Eusebius reports what Constantine told him long afterward. The emperor said he saw a cross of light in the sky, and his whole army saw it too. Within a year, toleration was law.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the vision Constantine saw, as Eusebius tells it, which the emperor told to him himself.
documented_stories.telling:
Eusebius tells what Constantine himself told him, long afterward and under oath. While he was on campaign, about noon, Constantine said he saw with his own eyes a cross of light in the sky above the sun. It carried the words "Conquer by this." His whole army, he said, saw it too.

That night, Eusebius says, Christ appeared to Constantine in his sleep with the same sign. Christ commanded him to make a standard of it and to carry it before his armies. Constantine did so, and then came the battle at the Milvian Bridge.

Eusebius reports what a ruler wanted remembered about his own rise, and he wrote it after that ruler's death.

Constantine stopped hunting the church, and within a year toleration was law.
documented_stories.title: Eusebius and the Cross of Light

documented_stories.teaser: In a church quarrel in Africa, Constantine does not send troops. He leaves one side holding a basilica he had built, and pays for another church for the Catholics.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the year the emperor lost an argument with a church and paid for a second building rather than send soldiers
documented_stories.telling:
When Constantine stepped into the quarrel in Africa's church, he did what emperors do and called a hearing. The matter had already been heard at Rome. In 314 he sent Caecilian and his accusers to Arles, and the councils duly ruled against the Donatists.

It settled nothing. Sixteen years later, in 330, the Donatists still held basilicas that the Catholics said belonged to them. One of those buildings was a church that Constantine had built himself, for Catholic use.

He wrote to the bishops of Numidia about it, but he did not order the buildings seized, and he did not send troops. He left the Donatists where they were. The Catholic bishops had asked for another site instead, and he granted it. He paid for a new church to be built there for the Catholics, once again at his own expense.

He also ordered that the Catholic lower clergy be freed again from forced public service, which the Donatists had maneuvered them into.
documented_stories.title: Constantine Builds a Second Church for Africa's Catholics

documented_stories.teaser: A council in the East removes Athanasius. Julius, bishop of Rome, says the custom is to write to Rome first.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Julius's letter of 341, the earliest surviving voice of Rome's claim to lead, kept by the man it helped
documented_stories.telling:
A council in the East had condemned Athanasius of Alexandria and removed him from office. Julius, bishop of Rome, was expected to accept that decision. Instead he wrote back, questioning the council's right to settle the matter before Rome had heard it.

He put it to them as a question. "Are you unaware that the custom has been to write to us first, and then for a just decision to be passed from this place?" Julius had not attended their council. Those he wrote to disputed how old and settled that custom was.
documented_stories.title: Julius of Rome Writes to the East

documented_stories.teaser: Symmachus, prefect of Rome, asks the young emperor to bring back the Altar of Victory. Ambrose answers him twice in writing. The altar stays removed.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the Altar of Victory debate of 384 - the old religion's most eloquent plea, and the church's answer, both in their own words
documented_stories.telling:
The altar of Victory stood in the Senate house in Rome. Constantius had it removed and Julian put it back, and then Gratian removed it again.

In the year 384, Symmachus petitioned the young emperor to bring the altar back. He was prefect of Rome and the old religion's most eloquent voice. Rome's ancient worship, he said, had guarded Rome's ancient greatness, and so great a secret could not be reached by one road alone.

Ambrose answered him twice in writing. A Christian emperor's state, Ambrose argued, may not fund what the faith knows to be false. What Symmachus called reverence for the past was, to Ambrose, the past's own long error.

The altar stayed removed.
documented_stories.title: The Altar of Victory: Rome's Old Religion Makes Its Case

documented_stories.teaser: Acting under a new law, the imperial court wants a church in Milan for its own confession. Ambrose refuses. The people stay inside with him and sing, and the court does not take it.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the 386 standoff in Milan, where a congregation held its church against the court and sang.
documented_stories.telling:
The imperial court wanted one of Milan's churches for the worship of its own confession, the one that said "like the Father" and no more. The court was acting under an imperial law of January 386, which let that confession assemble for worship. The printed edition of Ambrose's letters dates the law a year earlier.

Ambrose would not give the church up. As he told his sister, "I cannot give up the basilica, but I must not fight."

Soldiers came and stood around the building. Ambrose stayed inside with the people, and the people stayed with him. Augustine was in the city, and he remembered it plainly. The pious people, he wrote, kept guard in the church, ready to die with their bishop.

It was then, Augustine says, that Milan began to sing hymns and psalms in the manner of the Eastern churches. They sang so that the people would not waste away in the weariness of sorrow. He wrote that the custom was kept from then on, and that nearly all congregations across the world copied it.

In the middle of the standoff, Ambrose preached that "the Emperor is within the Church, not above it." The court did not take the building.
documented_stories.title: A Milan Congregation Holds Its Church

documented_stories.teaser: Christians burn a synagogue at Callinicum. The emperor orders the bishop to pay for a new one, but Ambrose gets the order changed.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the 388 fight over a burned synagogue, where Ambrose used his power to shield the guilty.
documented_stories.telling:
At Callinicum, on the eastern frontier, Christians burned the town's synagogue, and it was reported that the local bishop had urged it. In a separate attack, monks burned a meeting house of the Valentinians.

Theodosius heard of it and ordered the usual remedy. The bishop would pay to rebuild the synagogue, and the monks would be punished.

Ambrose wrote to the emperor himself to get the order reversed. He did not deny the burning. He judged it unbearable for a bishop to be forced to pay for a synagogue. He judged it worse that anyone should answer for burning the Valentinian house, which he likened to a heathen temple.

When the order stood, Ambrose preached in front of Theodosius in church. He refused to offer the sacrament until the emperor promised, then and there, to change the order and end the inquiry. Theodosius gave in.

His refusal protected the people who set the fire, and they never had to pay for what they burned.
documented_stories.title: Ambrose Defends the Men Who Burned a Synagogue

documented_stories.teaser: The emperor's soldiers kill a crowd. Ambrose writes that he dares not offer the sacrifice if the emperor is there. Later writers say the emperor did public penance.
documented_stories.tellable_as: a massacre and an emperor's penance. Ambrose's own letter comes first, and the famous later scene is kept apart.
documented_stories.telling:
In the year 390, a riot in Thessalonica killed one of the emperor's generals. Theodoret writes that in his rage Theodosius ordered a reprisal. His soldiers massacred the crowd in the circus with no trial, cutting down innocent and guilty together. It is said, Theodoret adds, that seven thousand died.

Ambrose wrote to the emperor in his own hand, for his eyes alone, and says he chose private words over public ones. "I, I say, have no reason to charge you with defiance, but I have reason to fear," he wrote. "I dare not offer the sacrifice if you intend to be present."

He asked whether what is not allowed after one innocent person's blood is shed could be allowed after the blood of many. He wanted the emperor's repentance shown before he stood at the altar again.

Two church historians, Sozomen and Theodoret, say that Theodosius did it. Decades later they tell the famous scene. In it the emperor lays aside his purple robes and weeps for his sin in the church at Milan.
documented_stories.title: Thessalonica and the Emperor's Penance

documented_stories.teaser: Eutropius, the emperor's chamberlain, has ended the church's right of refuge. When he falls, he runs to the altar himself. Bishop John shelters him and preaches on his ruin. Eutropius is later executed.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the day the man who abolished sanctuary had to use it - and the bishop who let him
documented_stories.telling:
Eutropius was a eunuch who rose to be chamberlain to the emperor Arcadius, and in 399 he became the first eunuch ever made consul. With that power he obtained laws that cut off the church's ancient right of refuge, so that a fugitive at the altar could be taken.

Then he fell. He ran to the Great Church and took hold of the altar, the one protection he had himself destroyed, and the soldiers came for him.

The bishop, John, preached with Eutropius lying there. In front of the man and the whole city, he preached the emptiness of everything Eutropius had spent his life getting. Where is the consulship now, he asked, and where are the torches and the swarm of people who flattered him?

Then John turned on his own congregation, who wanted the man handed over. He told them they were servants of a crucified man who had said, forgive them. Yes, he granted, this is the man who abolished refuge here, and he has learned by experience what he did.

The emperor held the army off, but the protection did not last. Eutropius left the church and was taken, and later he was exiled and executed. John preached a second time, about that too.
documented_stories.title: The Man Who Abolished Sanctuary Has to Use It

documented_stories.teaser: At Chalcedon the bishops cry out that Peter has spoken through Leo's Tome. Weeks later the council ranks Constantinople next after Rome, and Leo refuses it.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Leo's Tome at Chalcedon, and the canon he would not receive - our closing argument, left open
documented_stories.telling:
Leo did not go to Chalcedon. His legates went in his place, and his letter, the Tome, was read to the assembled bishops. The session record has them crying out, "This is the faith of the fathers," and then, "Peter has spoken so through Leo."

Not every bishop was satisfied. The Tome was questioned in session and compared with the teaching of Cyril.

Three weeks later, the same council did something else. It gave Constantinople equal privileges with old Rome and a rank just after her. It also gave Constantinople the right to ordain the chief bishops of three regions.

No apostle had taught there, and the canon gave a different reason. Earlier bishops had rightly granted privileges to old Rome as the royal city, and the new royal city should be honored the same way.

Leo's legates objected in the council itself. When word reached Leo, he refused to accept the canon and wrote to the emperor, the empress and the bishop of Constantinople. To the emperor he wrote that "things secular stand on a different basis from things divine." Constantinople was a royal city, he said, but it could never be an apostolic see.
documented_stories.title: The Tome Is Acclaimed and Canon 28 Is Refused

floor_note.text: This world did not merely inherit the Nicene confession. It is where that confession was made. The council of Nicaea itself sits inside this world's own window, in 325. But holding that word, homoousios, "of one substance," was never simple, even here. For roughly two decades, the empire's own church confessed the rival word instead. It held the Son was merely "like" the Father. The bishops who refused that word were the ones sent into exile. Even Eusebius of Caesarea, present at Nicaea itself, wrote home to explain his own hesitation over the word he had just signed. This world is remembered for defending that confession. But inside its own establishment, it was an argued position - and sometimes a losing one. It was never a settled starting point.

highlights.note: Bishop of Milan from 374 until his death in 397. A former provincial governor, he was chosen bishop by the people of Milan.
Emperor who won at the Milvian Bridge in 312. He called the council at Nicaea in 325. He was baptized as he lay dying, in 337.
Bishop of Caesarea and the emperor's historian. He wrote a life of Constantine after the emperor died. It praises its hero and leaves some things out.
A Christian writer who taught at Constantine's court. His account of the dream is the earlier one.
Rome held that what was given to Peter passed to each later bishop in his seat. Its standing was an inheritance.
Bishop of Alexandria. A council in the East deposed him. Years later he quoted Julius's letter of 341 to defend himself.
Bishop of Rome from 337 to 352. His letter of 341 claimed Rome's right to review other churches' judgments.
Constantine's son, and sole emperor from 353 to 361. Under him the imperial church said the Son is like the Father.
Emperor of the East from 364 to 378. Under him the Homoian creed ruled again, and bishops loyal to Nicaea went into exile once more.
Emperor from 379 to 395. He made the Nicene faith the law of the empire. His soldiers killed a crowd at Thessalonica in 390.
A young professor in Milan in 386. He recalled the standoff in his Confessions.
A bishop whose church history covers 325 to 429. He tells the fullest story of the penance, written decades later.
A lawyer who wrote a church history. He tells of the penance decades after it.
Bishop of Rome from 440 to 461. He wrote the Tome in 449. Leo did not attend Chalcedon.
Prefect of Rome in 384 and a pagan senator.
Chamberlain to the emperor Arcadius. In 399 he became the first eunuch to be made consul.

highlights.label: John Chrysostom
highlights.note: John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople from 398. He preached on Eutropius twice in 399, the first time with the man at the altar before him.
From homoios, meaning like. The creed that the Son is like the Father, as the scriptures say. For years it was the empire's official faith.
The faith set out at the council of Nicaea. Its key word says the Son shares the Father's own being.
A law that let Christians and all others follow the religion each thought best. Constantine and Licinius agreed it at Milan in 313.
A large hall-style church. Emperors began to fund such buildings, and in Milan in 386 one became the prize in a fight.
Here it means the Eucharist, which a bishop offers at the altar.
Envoys who spoke for Leo at the council, since he stayed away.
A letter that settles doctrine and carries the full weight of the church that sends it. Leo's reached Chalcedon without him.
A rule passed at Chalcedon. It ranked the emperor's city next after Rome, since he reigned there. Leo refused it.
A see is a bishop's seat. Rome held Peter's seat. No apostle had founded Constantinople.
An old altar in the Senate house at Rome. In 384 Symmachus asked the emperor to bring it back.

highlights.label: Constantinople
highlights.note: In the canon this means Constantinople. It was called New Rome, since the emperor ruled from it.
Constantine founded this city in 330 as the capital of the East. Today it is Istanbul, in Turkey.
First a Celtic town, it later became a Western Roman capital. Today it is Milan, in Italy. Ambrose was its bishop.
A Roman bridge over the Tiber River, now called Ponte Milvio, in Italy. Constantine won a battle here in 312.
A port city in Egypt's Nile Delta. Athanasius was its bishop.
A city in northern Greece, now Thessaloniki. In 390 a massacre took place here. Ambrose told the emperor to repent.
The city where the council of 451 met. Its site is now Kadıköy, in Turkey.
A town on the eastern frontier where a synagogue was burned in 388. It may be the same place as Nicephorium, now Raqqa in Syria.

legacy.text: This world's own final council did not close in agreement. Chalcedon's settlement on Christ's two natures was final for those who accepted it. But whole regions rejected it at once, starting in Egypt, at the council itself. This rejection did not fade the way earlier disputes had. It hardened into lasting division. This world's own record ends right as that fracture opens. It does not know how the fracture will end.

The two rival claims this world argued over never stopped being argued over. Does this world's own record already amount to a settled papacy? Or is it a claim still being worked out? Later traditions still argue that question, from these same documents. Constantinople's own rank raises a second, related fight. This world's own closing council granted that rank on one ground: nearness to the throne, not an apostle's grave. The tradition that received the rank reads it one way. The see that refused it reads it another way. This world's own record opens that disagreement. It does not close it.

read_first.note: This world's richest single voice on the alliance's own limits - the basilica standoff, Callinicum, and the emperor's penance all told from inside. One man's own record of his own confrontations; treat its consistency as a risk, not automatic proof.

source.citation: Ambrose of Milan, Selected Epistles, trans. H. de Romestin, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 10 (1896)

read_first.note: The see of Rome's fullest surviving voice, closing in the Tome and the Canon 28 rejection - documents that assert the very authority they are offered as evidence for.

source.citation: Leo I, bishop of Rome, Letters, trans. Charles Lett Feltoe, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 12 (1895)

read_first.note: This world's own closing scene in its own words: the Tome received, and the canon Rome's own legates refused on the spot, both preserved in the same conciliar record.

source.citation: The Council of Chalcedon (451), Definition of Faith, Canons and Acts, ed. and trans. Henry R. Percival, The Seven Ecumenical Councils, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 14 (1900)

relations_summary.text: This world argued with real rivals, not invented ones. Inside the church itself, for roughly two decades, the Homoian confession held the imperial throne. It was not a fringe opponent working from outside power. It was the establishment. Its rivals had to work against it from underneath. In Africa, a separate church called the Donatists claimed to be the true church. They held basilicas the Catholics claimed as their own. Constantine's own courts ruled against them twice. Even so, the emperor paid to build a second church, rather than send troops. On the eastern frontier, monks burned a meeting-house that belonged to a different Christian group, the Valentinians. A mob burned a synagogue on the very same day. And outside the church altogether, in 384, Rome's last great pagan senator made his own case in writing. He argued that the old gods' rites should be restored to the Senate house. This is a rare moment. This world's record keeps its own defeated opponent's case, in his own words, answered right beside it rather than erased.

sourcing.text: This world's record is richest in one shape: the paper trail of office. Council acts, church laws, imperial laws, and letters between bishops and emperors carry nearly everything that survives. Elsewhere, it runs thin, or falls silent. No ordinary believer's own words about any event survive. Only bishops, emperors, and their courts speak. Women show up as real political powers, not just as obstacles. But they never speak in their own words. Even the two who held real, proven power reach us only through men with their own stake in the story. And for roughly two decades, the empire's own church held a creed whose own fullest voice barely survives at all. We know it mostly through the side that later beat it.

story.text: From 312 to 451, in Rome, Constantinople and Milan, the church fought over who had the last word. The emperor, a council and the bishop of Rome each had a claim. Three answers competed over what that authority rested on. Rome traced its standing to the apostle Peter. Constantinople based its rank on being near the emperor. Ambrose of Milan held that a bishop's sacraments and moral standing gave him leverage over any ruler.

In 312 Constantine fought the battle at the Milvian Bridge. Eusebius tells what Constantine himself told him long afterward. About noon, he said, he saw a cross of light with the words "Conquer by this." His whole army, he said, saw it too. Lactantius wrote earlier and tells it differently. In his account a dream told Constantine to mark Christ's sign on his soldiers' shields. The emperor stopped hunting the church, and within a year toleration was law.

A council in the East deposed Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria. In 341 Julius, bishop of Rome, wrote back that the custom was to write to Rome first. Those he wrote to disputed how old and settled that custom was.

Imperial favor did not stay with one creed. Under Constantius II the empire's own church confessed that the Son is like the Father. That creed is called Homoian. Valens enforced it again in the East. For roughly two decades it was the official faith, and bishops who held the Nicene faith were deposed and exiled.

Ambrose set a limit on the alliance. In 386 the imperial court wanted one of his churches for the Homoian confession it held. It acted under a law of January 386 allowing Homoians to assemble for worship. The printed edition of Ambrose's letters dates the law a year earlier. Ambrose refused to give the church up. "I cannot give up the basilica, but I must not fight," he told his sister. Soldiers stood around the building, and Ambrose stayed inside with the people. Augustine, then in the city, remembered that they kept guard, ready to die with their bishop. He wrote that Milan then began to sing hymns and psalms in the Eastern way. Ambrose preached that the emperor is within the Church, not above it. The court did not take the building.

In 388 Christians burned the synagogue at Callinicum, on the eastern frontier. Theodosius ordered the local bishop to pay for a new one. Ambrose would not offer the sacrament until the emperor promised to change the order. Theodosius gave in. Here Ambrose used his power to shield the people who set the fire.

In 390 a riot at Thessalonica killed one of the emperor's generals. Theodosius ordered revenge, and his soldiers killed a crowd in the circus with no trial. Theodoret writes that seven thousand are said to have died. Ambrose sent the emperor a private letter. "I dare not offer the sacrifice if you intend to be present," he wrote. He asked the emperor to repent before he stood at the altar again. Decades later, Sozomen and Theodoret wrote that he did public penance.

Leo of Rome did not go to the council at Chalcedon in 451. His legates went in his place, and his letter, the Tome, was read. The session record has the bishops crying out that Peter has spoken so through Leo. Three weeks later the council passed Canon 28. It gave Constantinople privileges equal to old Rome's, and rank just after her. Earlier bishops, it said, had rightly given Rome privileges because it was the royal city. The new royal city, it said, should be honored the same way. Leo's legates objected, and Leo refused the canon. He wrote to the emperor that things secular stand on a different basis from things divine. He said Constantinople was a royal city and could never be an apostolic see.

dates.floruit: victor at the Milvian Bridge 312; the Milan agreement 313; convened Nicaea 325; dedicated Constantinople 330

names.name: Constantine I ("the Great", c. 272/273-337, sole emperor 324-337)

voices.hedge: Two accounts of what turned Constantine toward Christ survive. This world's own record does not force them to agree. One was written within a few years, by a Christian at his own court. The other came decades later, from his own admiring biographer. That later account has Constantine and his whole army seeing a vision at midday. What is certain is the alliance that followed - not the experience behind it.
voices.text: Constantine won the battle that made him sole ruler of the West, and turned an empire that had hunted the church into one that funded it. Within a year of his victory, toleration was law. He convened the council of Nicaea and called himself a bishop of those outside the church. He was baptized only on his deathbed, decades later.

dates.floruit: provincial governor, then bishop of Milan by popular acclamation 374 - elected while still an unbaptized catechumen, baptized and consecrated within about a week (an irregular path remarkable enough to be recorded, not a general rule); the Altar of Victory exchange 384; the basilica standoff 386; Callinicum 388; Thessalonica and the emperor's penance 390

voices.hedge: Almost everything we know of Ambrose comes from his own account of his own fights. The 386 standoff does have a real witness from outside - Augustine's own memory. Not every event does. And this world's own record will not let him look good every time. The same tool that once made an emperor kneel also once shielded men who had burned a Jewish community's synagogue.
voices.text: Ambrose, bishop of Milan, held a basilica against an emperor's own soldiers. He preached that the emperor stands inside the church, not above it. Four years later, he used that same sacramental leverage again. This time he forced an emperor into public penance for a massacre. And two years before that, he used the same leverage a third time. That time, he shielded men who had burned a synagogue - so they never had to pay for it.

dates.born: c. 305 (scholarly convention; Jerome's notice says he died "at the age of almost eighty")
dates.died: 384, "in the reign of the Emperor Theodosius" (Jerome, De Viris 103, verified)
dates.floruit: bishop of Rome 366-384; the martyr-epigram program; the see's self-presentation as guardian of apostolic memory

voices.hedge: This world tells that hard fact about Damasus's own election. It does not hide it. A body of decrees also circulates under his name. They are not used here. Modern scholarship judges much of that corpus a later forgery, backdated to look older than it is. His genuine synodical letters, and his own verse-inscriptions, carry his record instead.
voices.text: Damasus, bishop of Rome, built the see's own claim into stone. He paid for verses to be carved at the martyrs' graves. Pilgrims could then read Rome's own memory of its descent from the apostles. His own election, in 366, turned violent. A hostile pagan witness records a hundred and thirty-seven dead, in one church, in one day.

dates.died: 461 - a decade past this world's own 451 close; his death is outside the window and nothing after Chalcedon's immediate aftermath is this world's to narrate
dates.floruit: bishop of Rome 440-461; the Tome to Flavian 449; Chalcedon and the Canon 28 rejection 451-452

names.name: Leo I ("the Great"), bishop of Rome (440-461)

voices.hedge: Leo's own letters assert the very authority they are offered as evidence for. A bishop of Rome states his own standing, in his own words. Did the wider church actually accept that claim as settled? Or was it only ever stated, never fully agreed? This world's own closing argument, Canon 28, leaves that question open.
voices.text: Leo, bishop of Rome, wrote the letter that closed this world's own argument over Christ's two natures. It was read aloud at Chalcedon. Those who received it well heard it as the see of Peter speaking. Leo then refused that same council's ruling on Constantinople's own rank. He wrote to the emperor, the empress, and the bishop alike, to say so.

dates.floruit: exercising a mother's dominant influence over the young Valentinian II at Milan - no formal regency title is attested; the Homoian court's principal in the 386 basilica demand

names.name: Justina (d. c. 388), empress, mother and dominant influence over the young Valentinian II

voices.hedge: Justina reaches us only through the writing of the bishop who defeated her. His own letter names the emperor, not her, as the one who used that force. It is only this account's own chronology that names her instead. This world states that difference. It does not resolve it.
voices.text: Justina was the mother of the young emperor Valentinian II. She was the real power behind him. She held the Homoian faith herself, and demanded a Milan basilica for it. When Ambrose refused, real force moved through her court. Merchants in the city were fined. People were locked up during Lent.

dates.floruit: Augusta 414; with Marcian from 450 the convening power behind Chalcedon 451

names.name: Aelia Pulcheria (399-453), Augusta from 414, empress with Marcian from 450

voices.hedge: Leo's letters address Pulcheria as a real political power, not as a courtesy. That is direct evidence of her own agency. But nothing of her own words survives anywhere in this world's record - not on her own terms, not anywhere.
voices.text: Pulcheria became empress in 414. She was one of two people whose own convening power actually brought about the Council of Chalcedon, in 451. Leo himself records that she commanded the council to be held. He had asked to hold it in Italy instead. She refused. He answered by sending his legates anyway, without protest.

tile.text: Between 312 and 451 CE, the Christian church in Rome, Constantinople, and Milan went from a hunted community to a partner of imperial power. In 312 the emperor Constantine allied himself with a church he had once persecuted. Bishops now gathered in councils an emperor summoned and paid for. The church gained legal standing, wealth, and a seat near the throne. It also had to decide what that nearness would cost. Three claims competed for who held final authority in the church. Rome traced its standing back to the apostle Peter. Constantinople claimed rank because the emperor now reigned there. And Ambrose of Milan argued that the emperor stood inside the church, not above it. For roughly two decades, the empire's own church confessed that the Son is like the Father. That was the official faith, and bishops who refused it went into exile. This story closes at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, which settled who Christ is.
